newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea to slash tax revenue, spending.
newsitem.headline: South Korea to slash tax revenue, spending.

text.p: South Korea plans to slash tax revenues and government spending this year as part of belt-tightening measures to keep inflation under control as the economy slows, the finance minister said on Thursday.

The government will cut two trillion won from this year's budgeted tax revenues and reduce public spending by an additional one trillion won on top of an earlier announced one trillion won cut, Kang Kyong-shik said in a statement.
The statement was released ahead of a joint news conference by key economy ministers at 3.00 p.m. (0600 GMT).
This year's tax revenues were originally set at 74 trillion won against last year's 64.96 trillion won, the statement said.
One trillion won would be cut from spending on state companies and provincial governments. It showed the government's willingness to take the lead in reducing excessive spending, the statement said.
In January President Kim Young-sam said one trillion won would be cut from public spending this year.
State budget growth next year would be held within a single digit, compared with a 13.4 percent rise in 1997.
"The government will itself streamline its organisations and manpower and save budget spending through a structural reorganisation," the statement said.
It blamed rising energy imports for much of last year's current account deficit and urged conservation. However, the statement offered no concrete steps to brake the snowballing deficit.
Last year, the nation's current account deficit rose to $23.72 billion from a shortfall of $8.95 billion in 1995.
The statement said the government would rely on market mechanisms to overcome the crisis sparked by the collapse in January of Hanbo Steel Co.
Hanbo Steel, flagship of South Korea's the 14th-largest conglomerate, the Hanbo Group, collapsed under the weight of five trillion won of debts.
The statement also reaffirmed the government's promise to speed up financial reform, but offered no details.
